'''Wolfgang Rindler''' (18 May 1924 – 8 February 2019) was an Austrian [[physicist]] studying [[general relativity]]. He is known for introducing the term "[[event horizon]]" for the boundary of a black hole, [[Rindler coordinates]], and (in collaboration with [[Roger Penrose]]) for the use of [[spinors]] in general relativity. An honorary member of the [[Austrian Academy of Sciences]] and foreign member of the {{Interlanguage link|Accademia delle Scienze di Torino|it}},<ref>{{cite web|url=https://explorer.utdallas.edu/editprofile.php?pid=13580&onlyview=1|title=Wolfgang A. Rindler|publisher=University of Texas – Dallas|access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref> he was also a prolific textbook author.

==Life and career==
Born in Vienna on 18 May 1924, Wolfgang Rindler was the son of a lawyer. In 1938, his mother sent him to England through the auspices of the [[Kindertransport]] rescue of [[Jewish]] children from Germany and Austria. He gained his B.Sc. and M.Sc. from the [[University of Liverpool]] and his PhD from [[Imperial College London]]. From 1956 to 1963 he taught at [[Cornell University]].

In 1960 [[Oliver & Boyd]] and [[InterScience]] published his first book on [[special relativity]]. Reviewer [[Alfred Schild]] said it was an "excellent, clear and concise account" and "provided a sound balance between physical ideas, analytical formulae and space-time geometry".<ref>[[Alfred Schild]] (1961) [https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183524311 Review: Special Relativity], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 67(5):449,50 link from [[Project Euclid]]</ref> (1966, second edition)

In 1961 Rindler used the [[Length contraction|FitzGerald contraction]] as the premise of his article "Length contraction paradox".<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Rindler, Wolfgang|title=Length Contraction Paradox|journal=[[American Journal of Physics]]|year=1961|volume=29|issue=6|pages=365–366|doi=10.1119/1.1937789|bibcode = 1961AmJPh..29..365R }}</ref> The [[thought experiment]] is now called the [[ladder paradox]].

In September 1963 he took up a position at the newly founded [[Southwest Center for Advanced Studies]], the private research organization that in 1969 became the [[University of Texas at Dallas]], where he was one of the founding faculty members. He was based at UTD for the remainder of his career, eventually becoming professor emeritus. He was visiting scholar at [[King's College London]] for the academic year 1961–1962, at the [[University La Sapienza]] in Rome for 1968–1969,

In 1969 Springer published the first edition of his ''Essential Relativity: Special, General, and Cosmological''. The undergraduate [[textbook]] was lauded as a "refreshingly modern approach to the critical problem of ''teaching'' relativity theory."<ref>{{cite magazine | last1=Rindler | first1=Wolfgang | last2=Jacobs | first2=Kenneth C. | title=Essential Relativity: Special, General and Cosmological | magazine=Physics Today | publisher=AIP Publishing | volume=23 | issue=12 | year=1970 | issn=0031-9228 | doi=10.1063/1.3021868 | pages=47–48}}</ref> Another reviewer said it is "simply the best introduction" and is "filled with fabulous insights."<ref>Chris Hllman (1998) [http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/Administrivia/rel_booklist.html Are there any good books on relativity ?] from [[University of California, Riverside]]</ref> When the second edition appeared in 1977 a reviewer noted its treatment "reminiscent of [[Ernst Mach|Mach]]'s celebrated examination of the foundations of classical mechanics". On the other hand, the second edition "gives the barest hints of new developments" (models of neutron stars, in [[X-ray astronomy]], supernova explosions, and quasars).<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rindler | first1=Wolfgang | last2=Ohanian | first2=Hans C. | title=Essential Relativity: Special, General, and Cosmological | journal=American Journal of Physics | publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) | volume=45 | issue=12 | year=1977 | issn=0002-9505 | doi=10.1119/1.10693 | pages=1235| bibcode=1977AmJPh..45.1235R }}</ref> Later, another reviewer criticized it for the paucity of diagrams, but lauded the chapter on [[cosmology]] as "lyrical, philosophical, yet technical."<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rindler | first1=Wolfgang | last2=Greenberger | first2=Daniel M. |author-link2=Daniel Greenberger| title=Essential Relativity | journal=American Journal of Physics | publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) | volume=51 | issue=1 | year=1983 | issn=0002-9505 | doi=10.1119/1.13409 | pages=94| bibcode=1983AmJPh..51...94R }}</ref>

Rindler was a visiting scholar at the [[University of Vienna]] in 1975 and 1987, and at Churchill College, [[Cambridge University]], in 1990.

In 1982 [[Oxford University Press]] published ''Introduction to Special Relativity'', with the second edition in 1991. A reviewer noted that other books provide a better introduction and intuitive understanding, but that it "should provide a useful reference for most applications of special relativity: kinematics, optics, particle mechanics, electromagnetism and mechanics of continua."<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rindler | first1=Wolfgang | last2=Hoffman | first2=Lyle | title=Introduction to Special Relativity | journal=American Journal of Physics | publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) | volume=52 | issue=3 | year=1984 | issn=0002-9505 | doi=10.1119/1.13719 | pages=285| bibcode=1984AmJPh..52..285R }}</ref>

In 1984 [[Roger Penrose]] and Rindler published ''Spinors and Spacetime'', volume 1, on "two-spinor calculus and relativistic fields". [[Michał Heller]] wrote that ''Spinors and Spacetime'' "is both elementary and highly advanced. It begins on an almost graduate level but soon, step by step, reaches the highest standards of modern mathematical physics."<ref>[[Michał Heller]] (1985) [http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1986AcC....14..143P/0000144.000.html Review: ''Spinors and Spacetime'', volume 1], ''Acta Cosmologica'' 14: 143,4 from [[Astrophysics Data System]]</ref>

In 2001 Oxford University Press published ''Relativity: Special, General and Cosmological'', with a second edition in 2006. A reviewer noted "His writing is elegant, yet compact and logically precise." He was impressed with the "discussion of the internal structure of [[black hole]]s analyzed first in [[Schwarzschild coordinates]], and then in a masterful treatment of the [[Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates|Kruskal extension]]."<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rindler | first1=Wolfgang | last2=Salisbury | first2=Donald | title=Relativity: Special, General, and Cosmological | journal=American Journal of Physics | publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) | volume=71 | issue=10 | year=2003 | issn=0002-9505 | doi=10.1119/1.1622355 | pages=1085–1086| bibcode=2003AmJPh..71.1085R }}</ref>

Wolfgang Rindler died at the age of 94 on 8 February 2019.<ref>[https://www.utdallas.edu/news/faculty/ut-dallas-remembers-founding-faculty-member-wolfgang-rindler/ Wolfgang Rindler, founding faculty member] from [[University of Texas at Dallas]]</ref>
